author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A 1956 satire set in a puritanical postwar society governed by moral surveillance, where a propaganda executive begins committing acts of subversive mockery—'japing'—against the regime he serves, without at first understanding that he is the saboteur.
page_summary:
In the reconstructed society of Morec (Moral Reclamation), citizens are watched by roving robot 'juveniles' that report every lapse, and public virtue is enforced through relentless social pressure. Allen Purcell, a rising executive in the propaganda apparatus who is about to be handed control of the state media, discovers that someone has been defacing a statue of the society's founder and committing other acts of ridicule. The culprit, he slowly realizes, is himself—acting in a fractured, unacknowledged capacity against the very order he administers.

The novel is early Dick working the theme of surveillance as internalized control: a regime that governs less through violence than through the constant possibility of being observed and reported, until citizens police their own thoughts. 'Japing'—satire, mockery, the deliberate puncturing of official piety—becomes the one available form of resistance, and Dick locates it in a protagonist divided against himself, prefiguring the split, self-monitoring consciousnesses of his later work.

Published by Ace in 1956, it is a slight but pointed satire, notable for how early Dick fixed on the idea that the most effective tyranny is the one its subjects carry inside their own heads.
